question: What is the main goal of patient safety in healthcare?

options.A: To eliminate the cost of hospital stays
options.B: To ensure doctors make all clinical choices
options.C: To speed up the hospital discharge process
options.D: To prevent accidental harm to patients

explanation: Patient safety is all about keeping patients protected from accidental injury or harm while they are receiving care from us. You've got this! [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h1)

question: Why are modern hospitals moving away from just blaming individuals when mistakes happen?

options.A: Because fixing underlying system flaws prevents future errors better
options.B: Because hospital management no longer cares about errors
options.C: Because nurses refuse to complete incident reports
options.D: Because punishing workers stops all future mistakes

explanation: Looking at system problems instead of just pointing fingers helps fix the root cause so the same mistake doesn't happen again. Great nursing practice starts with understanding this! [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h1)

question: What do we call a close call in the clinical area where a mistake almost happens?

options.A: A deliberate action taken to bypass hospital safety rules
options.B: An event that almost causes harm but is caught before reaching the patient
options.C: An unavoidable complication of a severe surgical procedure
options.D: An error that reaches the patient and causes mild pain

explanation: A near miss is your lucky break! It's when an error almost reaches the patient, but quick action or alertness stops it just in time. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h2)

question: A nurse draws up the wrong dose of insulin, but catches the mistake before giving it to the patient. What is this called?
explanation: Spotting the mistake before the injection means no harm was done. That's a classic near miss—phew! [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h2)

question: What is preventable harm in healthcare?

options.A: Allergic reactions to drugs with no prior history of allergy
options.B: Unavoidable side effects of a necessary surgical operation
options.C: Natural progression of a terminal disease without treatment
options.D: Damage caused by failing to follow accepted standards of care

explanation: Preventable harm is injury that could have been avoided if standard safety practices were properly followed. Every check we do counts! [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h3)

question: Which of these best describes permanent harm?

options.A: A temporary drop in blood pressure after changing positions
options.B: A lasting disability or loss of function caused by an error
options.C: A mild headache that resolves after sleeping overnight
options.D: An allergic rash that disappears after taking an antihistamine

explanation: Permanent harm means the patient suffers a long-term or irreversible loss of ability. This is why our daily safety checks are so important. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h3)

question: In the famous Swiss Cheese Model, what do the holes in the cheese slices represent?

options.A: Active weaknesses or gaps in safety defenses
options.B: Natural symptoms of a progressing illness
options.D: Deliberate criminal acts committed by staff

explanation: Think of the holes as little gaps or weaknesses in our hospital safety checks that can occasionally let an error slip through. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h4)

question: According to the Swiss Cheese Model, when does a serious mistake actually reach the patient?

options.A: When a patient refuses to take prescribed medications
options.B: When a single nurse makes a minor mental calculation
options.C: When the holes in all layers of defense align at the same time
options.D: When hospital management removes all safety policies

explanation: Errors usually happen not because of one person, but when multiple safety checks all fail at the exact same time, lining up their gaps. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h4)

question: Which of these is one of the most common types of errors in clinical practice?
explanation: Giving or managing medications happens all day, every day in nursing, which makes medication errors one of the most frequent types of clinical mistakes. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h5)

question: What is a common myth about medication administration errors?

options.A: They only occur in busy surgical operating rooms
options.B: They are always the sole fault of the nurse at the bedside
options.C: They never result in any negative physical outcomes
options.D: They are completely eliminated by electronic health records

explanation: Even though the nurse gives the drug, the root cause might actually go back to prescribing, pharmacy dispensing, or unclear packaging! [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h5)

question: What do we mean by the 'second victim' in healthcare?

options.A: The family members who witness a patient's decline
options.B: The secondary patient sharing a room with the affected individual
options.C: The healthcare professionals who experience emotional trauma after an error
options.D: The hospital institution that faces lawsuits and financial fines

explanation: The 'second victim' is the nurse or doctor who suffers deep emotional pain and stress after being involved in an unexpected patient incident. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h6)

question: How does a hospital's poor response to a nursing mistake affect the rest of the team?

options.A: It immediately prevents all future near misses
options.B: It improves patient trust in hospital management
options.C: It drives staff to leave the profession out of fear and burnout
options.D: It encourages open communication and total honesty

explanation: When hospitals rely on blame and punishment instead of support, staff live in fear, leading to burnout and nursing shortages. We need supportive wards! [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of a Root Cause Analysis (RCA)?

options.A: To assign blame and punishment to negligent staff members
options.B: To calculate the financial cost of patient lawsuits
options.C: To investigate why an error occurred by identifying underlying system flaws
options.D: To evaluate the daily bedside performance of individual students

explanation: RCA is like detective work! It looks deep into the system to find out why a mistake happened, rather than just pointing fingers at a person. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h7)

question: Why is an open reporting culture so important for fixing hospital errors?

options.A: It allows the hospital to fire careless workers quickly
options.B: It eliminates the need for written nursing documentation
options.C: It provides the data needed to understand and fix system flaws
options.D: It ensures nurses receive immediate financial bonuses

explanation: Without honest reports from nurses on the floor, management cannot see where the system is breaking down or how to fix it. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h7)

question: What does a 'just culture' in nursing try to balance?

options.A: Accountability for choices with understanding of system flaws
options.B: Zero documentation with total reliance on verbal handovers
options.C: Strict punishment for every single near miss that occurs
options.D: Financial profit margins with patient satisfaction scores

explanation: A just culture is fair: it holds people responsible for reckless choices, but supports them when honest human errors or system flaws happen. [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h8)

question: A junior nurse notices a senior doctor prescribing the wrong drug dose, but stays quiet out of fear. What concept is lacking in this unit?
explanation: Psychological safety means every team member feels safe speaking up and asking questions, no matter their rank. Your voice matters in patient care! [learn more](GST319_U5_T5#GST319_U5_T5_h8)
